title: The Shape of Prices
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Prices tell a story about an economy, and the prices in the imaginary country of Calderia, recorded every month for ten years by the national statistics office, tell several stories at once. Some goods have become steadily more expensive, some have become cheaper, and some have moved up and down without any clear direction. Economists study such patterns in order to understand why prices change, and shoppers study them in order to decide when to buy. This passage looks at four goods in the office's records: tomatoes, petrol, bread and laptop computers. Each follows its own pattern, and the reasons for each are quite different.

The price of tomatoes goes up and down all the time. It is lowest in late summer, when the harvest is large and the shops are full of fruit grown in the open air, and highest in winter, when tomatoes must be grown in heated greenhouses or brought from abroad. Over the ten years there was no real upward or downward trend, only a regular rise and fall with the seasons, and occasional sudden jumps after bad weather destroyed crops. Shoppers who want to save money have learned to buy in bulk when prices are low and to preserve the fruit in jars for the colder months.

Petrol was cheap and stable for most of the period. For seven years its price hardly moved, and drivers grew used to filling their tanks without thinking about the cost. Then, in the eighth year, the price rose sharply, after a war in a distant oil-producing region cut supplies, and within eighteen months it had almost doubled. It has since crept up a little further. The effect on the economy was immediate: transport companies raised their charges, and the prices of many other goods followed, which shows how much modern life depends on the cost of fuel.

The price of bread followed another pattern. It rose quickly during the first four years, as the cost of wheat, flour and energy increased, and then it reached a level at which it stayed. The government, worried that poor families could not afford their daily bread, froze the price and paid bakers a subsidy to cover the difference. The policy has been popular, but it is expensive, costing the treasury about the same each year as the building of a hundred new schools. Some economists argue that the money would be better spent giving direct help to poor families, rather than keeping the price of one product artificially low.

Laptop computers have become cheaper, but the fall came suddenly, not gradually. For the first six years, their price stayed almost the same, because only two companies sold them in the country, and neither wanted to start a price war. Then a new factory opened in the south, and several foreign makers entered the market. Within a few months, the average price fell by nearly half, and it has stayed at the lower level ever since. Competition, in other words, can change a market far more quickly than any government order, which is a lesson that economists often repeat.

Dr Anita Rossi, a professor of economics, says that the four cases illustrate the main forces behind prices: the seasons, supply, government decisions and competition. When supply is limited, as with petrol after the war, prices rise; when many sellers compete, as with laptops, they fall. She warns, however, that people often misunderstand the pattern they see. A rise in the price of a single product, she says, is not inflation, which is a general rise in the cost of living, and a fall in one price does not always mean that people are better off, since the money saved may be lost somewhere else in the economy.

The statistics office has recently made its figures available to the public on a website, and thousands of people now use them. Teachers use the charts in lessons, journalists use them in articles, and ordinary families use them to plan their budgets. The office's director says that the aim is to make economics less mysterious: when citizens can see for themselves how prices move, he argues, they are less likely to be misled by rumours or by claims made in advertisements. Next year the website will add figures for wages, so that visitors can compare the cost of goods with the amount of money that people actually earn.
